ioQWjgvKTDE.title: Reflections on the Farewell Sermon and the Rituals of Hajj
ioQWjgvKTDE.one_line: Why pilgrims stone the jamarat: Adam's and Ibrahim's encounters with Shaytan, submission to Allah's command, and holding to the perfected religion.
ioQWjgvKTDE.summary: Delivered in the days of tashreeq, the khutbah starts from the verse on the perfection of religion revealed at Arafah and from the pilgrims stoning the jamarat that very day. Hajj, he says, is a journey of symbolism, and without understanding it pilgrims return unchanged. He tells two stories behind the stoning. Adam and Hawwa, new to having a will, slipped, lost everything and wandered until a moment of clarity at Arafah about who they were and what they hoped for; when Shaytan returned to tempt Adam again near Mina, Adam drove him off with pebbles. Centuries later Ibrahim, a man famous for questioning, was commanded in a dream to slaughter his only son and did not question it; father, son and Hajar each threw stones at Shaytan as he tried to argue them out of obedience. The lesson of the Eid sacrifice is that Allah never commanded anything against our interest, though we owe Him everything. Seven small stones signify continuity: Shaytan never stops, so resistance must be lifelong, and everyone will orbit some centre, so make it Allah. The second khutbah quotes the Farewell Sermon on the Basin and those who deviate, and warns against compromising a religion Allah already perfected; ijtihad only applies rulings to new contexts.

outline.heading: Opening
The perfected religion, revealed at Arafah
outline.gist: The verse completing the religion came on a Friday like this one while the Prophet stood at Arafah, a sign that his mission was done and his death near; today the pilgrims are throwing the jamarat.

outline.heading: Why throw the jamarat?
outline.gist: As Hajj ends, the stoning is the ritual that takes the most time, three days in Mina for perhaps an hour and a half of throwing; so why do pilgrims do it?

outline.heading: Hajj is a journey of symbolism
outline.gist: Without the symbolism it makes little sense; countless people have gone and come back without grasping what they were part of. The stories of Adam, even in Jannah, are tied to Hajj.

outline.heading: Adam and Hawwa: new to having a will
outline.gist: They were new to having a soul, following commands and relating to Allah; Shaytan offered an upgrade from mortal to immortal, and the fear of death made the illusion work.

outline.heading: They lost everything
outline.gist: Not yet knowing how to strive against the self, they slipped; everything was stripped away in a second and they wandered, lost physically or in not knowing how to fix it, until a moment of clarity.

outline.heading: Arafah: where Adam came to know
outline.gist: The place is named for knowing: there he learned why he was created, what it meant to be khalifah and father of all humanity, and Allah showed him his descendants.

outline.heading: Hoping for Jannah: why pilgrims walk the route
outline.gist: Asked what they hoped for, they said Jannah; pilgrims walk that road every year to immortalise the moment. Then Adam sets out from Mina toward the land Allah sent him to.

outline.heading: Shaytan, unseen, and his challenge over Adam
outline.gist: Jinn are unseen to us, whatever YouTube videos claim; only prophets are in touch with that realm. Shaytan rejected the rank Allah gave Adam, who had done nothing yet but carried potential.

outline.heading: Shaytan feels he is losing
outline.gist: He proved his point by getting them to do the one thing forbidden, which is far more than eating an apple; once they repented and changed course, he came back to make Adam disobey again.

outline.heading: Adam's pebbles, and a story with its own day
outline.gist: Adam threw six or seven pebbles at the whisperer and went on to lay the Kaaba's foundations. The second story is one we are obliged to reflect on one day each year, now reduced to paying for an udhiyah delivered to the door.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's dream
outline.gist: Slaughter a hady and think of what Ibrahim saw: while being taught Hajj he dreamt of slaughtering his only son, born after long waiting, old enough to help and devoted to Allah.

outline.heading: The dream returns; the son's answer
outline.gist: Ibrahim waited in case the first dream was from Iblis; when it recurred he asked his son, who said do as commanded, you will find me patient.

outline.heading: Full submission and the silent walk
outline.gist: Not accepting Islam but surrendering their own will; he laid his son on his forehead. Imagine the silent walk of father, mother and son toward the place, and go walk it yourself.

outline.heading: A command that made no sense to a man of logic
outline.gist: Ibrahim questioned everything, which is why he became the father of prophets; to be told to kill an innocent, believing only son is worse than any harm to oneself, as every parent knows.

outline.heading: We are owed nothing
outline.gist: There was no wisdom in the act itself, which is why it never happened; the lesson to all after him is to obey, since we are owed nothing and owe Him everything, and wisdom lies in every command.

outline.heading: This time he did not question
outline.gist: The same Ibrahim once asked to see how Allah gives life so his heart would be at rest; here he understood the test, laid his son down and struck, and the knife did not cut.

outline.heading: You have fulfilled the vision
outline.gist: Like the fire that did not burn and the sea that parted, it did not happen; Allah declares the vision fulfilled and says Ibrahim was tested and completed it. What were the three thinking on that walk?

outline.heading: Shaytan's three attempts
outline.gist: A command that feels impossible breeds a million righteous objections, and Shaytan exploits it: he comes to Ibrahim, then Ismail, then Hajar, and each throws seven pebbles at him.

outline.heading: The ram: never commanded what harms you
outline.gist: A ram is slaughtered instead; each Eid we sacrifice to remember He never commanded anything not in our interest, though He could have, and we would still owe obedience.

outline.heading: Ibrahim did it anyway
outline.gist: We know His commands serve us and still do not follow; Ibrahim said bismillah and went through with it. That is how a Muslim acts, and Eid is the reminder.

outline.heading: Seven: the symbol of continuity
outline.gist: The stones are small, not boulders; in Arabic usage seven signals continuity, like the week that starts over. It is not one big blow but a fight that never ends, because he never leaves you alone.

outline.heading: Seventy stones in all
outline.gist: He works through whims, arrogance, vanity, envy, indifference, hatred and selfishness, so you must keep fighting; three jamarat over three days plus the first day comes to seventy, seven again.

outline.heading: A centre, a goal, an enemy: choose them rightly
outline.gist: You will orbit some centre, work toward some goal and fight something all your life; make the centre Allah and the enemy Shaytan, because he will never stop.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Farewell Sermon: waiting at the Basin
outline.gist: The Prophet will wait at the Basin, hoping to show the numbers who followed him, but some will be pulled away, and he will be told he does not know how they deviated after him.

outline.heading: A perfected religion: ijtihad, not new values
outline.gist: Allah perfected the deen, so we seek only better insight into what the Prophet said and did; ijtihad never changes the religion, it understands a ruling within the current context so it keeps serving its purpose.

outline.heading: Do not sell out the basics
outline.gist: Shaytan will try to make people compromise and claim right and wrong are unclear, but the Prophet explained them; Hajj takes us back to those basics.

themes.label: Submission and obedience to Allah's command

themes.label: Tazkiyah: purifying and training the self

You have fulfilled the vision.

Shaytan came to Adam near Mina to tempt him again and Adam threw pebbles at him.
Shaytan appeared to Ibrahim, Ismail and Hajar at the three jamarat and each stoned him with seven pebbles.

Farewell Sermon: I will wait for you at the Basin and boast of your numbers, so do not disgrace me; some will be driven away and I will be told you do not know what they changed after you, and I will say away with them.

maxims: Hajj is a journey of symbolism
We are not owed anything; we owe Him everything
He never commanded anything not in your best interest
Seven symbolizes continuity
Make Allah your centre, or it will be something else
Ijtihad is understanding a ruling within the current context

stories.who: Adam and Hawwa
stories.point: Inexperience let them fall for the illusion of immortality; clarity at Arafah about purpose and hope is what Hajj re-enacts.

stories.who: Adam stoning Shaytan near Mina
stories.point: After repentance Shaytan tries again, so the believer must actively push him away.

stories.who: Ibrahim, Ismail and the dream of sacrifice
stories.point: Complete submission even when the command seems to have no wisdom; Allah never intended the harm.

stories.who: Ibrahim, Ismail and Hajar on the walk to the slaughter
stories.point: Shaytan offers a million objections that make disobedience feel righteous; each of them rejected him.

contemporary: Hajj 2023, the days of tashreeq, with pilgrims stoning the jamarat that day
Paying for udhiyah online instead of slaughtering and reflecting
YouTube videos claiming to show jinn
takeaways: Learn the symbolism of the Hajj rites so the worship changes you.
Obey Allah's commands even when you cannot see the wisdom, trusting that He commands only what benefits you.
Let the Eid sacrifice prompt real reflection on Ibrahim's submission, not just a payment.
Expect Shaytan's pressure to be lifelong and keep resisting in small, repeated acts.
Hold to the religion as perfected; seek better understanding of it rather than changing its values.
